period.label: Pleistocene to early Holocene

extinction.label: Final known island population disappeared about 4,000 years ago
extinction.note: The date refers to the small Wrangel Island population, not the disappearance of all mammoths at once.

causes.claim: Warming climate and habitat change reduced suitable steppe-tundra.
Human hunting contributed to some population declines.

habitat.text: Cold, open steppe-tundra environments.

geographicRange.text: Across northern Eurasia and North America; late surviving populations included Wrangel Island.

animals.livingRelatives: The Asian elephant (Elephas maximus) is the woolly mammoth's closest living relative.
animals.fossilDiscoveries: Mammoth remains are known from northern Eurasia and North America, including exceptionally preserved remains in Siberian permafrost. Wrangel Island fossils document a late-surviving population.
animals.appearance: A large elephant relative with a dense coat, small ears, a high-domed head, and long curved tusks.
animals.diet: Herbivore; grasses and other tundra plants.

size.text: Large; adult shoulder height varied by population.
size.estimate: Body size estimates vary; no single value is given here.

lastKnownRecord.text: Fossils show a small population survived on Wrangel Island until about 4,000 years ago.

interestingFacts: Some mammoth remains were preserved in permafrost.
The woolly mammoth was one of several mammoth species, not the only member of its genus.

image.creator: Anagoria

period.label: Pleistocene

extinction.label: Late Pleistocene; exact last appearance is not known
extinction.note: The end of the fossil record is not a documented last individual.

causes.claim: Climate and ecosystem changes at the end of the Pleistocene altered prey communities.
Human impacts may also have contributed.

habitat.text: A range of open and wooded habitats in the Americas.

geographicRange.text: North and South America.

animals.livingRelatives: No saber-toothed cat survives. Living cats (Felidae) are relatives at the family level, not descendants of Smilodon.
animals.fossilDiscoveries: Thousands of Smilodon fatalis fossils have been recovered from the Rancho La Brea asphalt deposits in California, including remains from multiple individuals.
animals.appearance: A powerfully built saber-toothed cat with very long upper canine teeth.
animals.diet: Carnivore.

size.text: Robust, large-bodied cat.
size.estimate: Mass and body-size estimates vary among specimens.

lastKnownRecord.text: No individual last record is known; the fossil record ends near the close of the Pleistocene.

interestingFacts: The common label 'saber-toothed tiger' is informal; Smilodon was not a tiger.
Smilodon fossils are abundant at the La Brea Tar Pits.

period.label: Historical era

extinction.label: By the late 17th century; exact final date is uncertain
extinction.note: Reported sightings after the mid-17th century are disputed.

causes.claim: Hunting, habitat change, and introduced animals affected the small island population.
causes.status: strongly implicated; the relative contribution of each factor is uncertain

habitat.text: Island forests and coastal lowlands of Mauritius.

geographicRange.text: Endemic to Mauritius in the Indian Ocean.

animals.livingRelatives: The Nicobar pigeon (Caloenas nicobarica) is among the closest living relatives identified by genetic studies; the extinct Rodrigues solitaire is another close relative.
animals.fossilDiscoveries: Subfossil bones from Mare aux Songes, Mauritius, provide important evidence about dodo anatomy and biology. Most finds are isolated or disarticulated bones rather than one complete skeleton.
animals.appearance: A large, flightless pigeon with a heavy bill and reduced wings; historical paintings differ in their details.
animals.diet: Likely included fruits, seeds, and other plant material; details are incompletely known.

size.text: A large ground-dwelling pigeon.
size.estimate: Body mass estimates vary and may have been affected by season and condition.

lastKnownRecord.text: No confirmed last individual is documented; the final date of survival remains uncertain.

interestingFacts: The dodo was a pigeon, not a member of a separate bird family.
No complete dodo skeleton from a single individual is known.

period.label: Historical era

extinction.label: Last known captive individual died in 1936
extinction.note: The exact date the species disappeared from the wild is unknown.

causes.claim: Government bounty hunting and persecution were major pressures in Tasmania.
Habitat changes and disease may also have contributed.

habitat.text: Forests, grasslands, and open woodland; habitat use varied across its former range.

geographicRange.text: Historically occurred on mainland Australia and New Guinea; survived into the historical period in Tasmania.

animals.livingRelatives: No thylacine survives. Tasmanian devils and quolls are living marsupial carnivores in the same broader order, but are not descendants of the thylacine.
animals.fossilDiscoveries: Fossils and subfossils from mainland Australia document a range beyond historical Tasmania; preserved skins, bones, photographs, and film record the recent population.
animals.appearance: A carnivorous marsupial with a stiff tail and dark transverse stripes across its hindquarters.
animals.diet: Carnivore; the full historical diet is not precisely known.

size.text: Medium-sized marsupial predator.
size.estimate: Adult measurements vary; estimates are based on surviving skins, skeletons, and records.

lastKnownRecord.text: The last known captive thylacine died at Hobart's Beaumaris Zoo in 1936.

interestingFacts: The thylacine was a marsupial, not a canid despite its skull's dog-like shape.
Historical film footage and photographs document living thylacines.

image.alt: 1891 illustrated spread from the Guide to the Gardens of the Zoological Society of London, showing two thylacines.
image.creator: M. A. Sclater and Philip Lutley

period.label: Historical era

extinction.label: Last known individual died on 1 September 1914
extinction.note: The individual, Martha, died at the Cincinnati Zoo.

causes.claim: Commercial-scale hunting and habitat loss caused a rapid population collapse.

habitat.text: Deciduous and mixed forests, especially where mast-producing trees were abundant.

geographicRange.text: Eastern and central North America.

animals.livingRelatives: Other pigeons and doves (Columbidae) are living relatives; no living species is a passenger pigeon descendant.
animals.fossilDiscoveries: The species is principally documented by historical accounts, photographs, and museum specimens, including the preserved remains of Martha at the Smithsonian.
animals.appearance: A slender pigeon with a long pointed tail; males and females differed in plumage.
animals.diet: Seeds, nuts, berries, and other plant foods.

size.text: A medium-sized pigeon, roughly 40 cm long.
size.estimate: Measurements vary among historical specimens.

lastKnownRecord.text: Martha, the last known passenger pigeon, died at the Cincinnati Zoo on 1 September 1914.

interestingFacts: Passenger pigeons once formed enormous migratory flocks, but flock size did not protect them from intensive hunting.
Martha's preserved remains are held by the Smithsonian.

period.label: Historical era

extinction.label: Last confirmed breeding pair killed in 1844
extinction.note: The pair was killed on Eldey, Iceland; reports of later sightings are unconfirmed.

causes.claim: Hunting for meat, feathers, and museum specimens drove the final decline.
Egg collection and disturbance at breeding colonies added pressure.

habitat.text: Rocky North Atlantic islands for breeding; open ocean for feeding.

geographicRange.text: North Atlantic coasts and islands.

animals.livingRelatives: Living auks, including the common murre (Uria aalge), are members of the same family and among its closest living relatives.
animals.fossilDiscoveries: Historical skins, eggs, and skeletons survive in museum collections; fossil remains also document the Great Auk's former North Atlantic range.
animals.appearance: A large, flightless auk with black-and-white plumage and a prominent white patch near the eye.
animals.diet: Marine fish and other sea prey.

size.text: About 75-85 cm tall.
size.estimate: Published measurements vary among historical specimens.

lastKnownRecord.text: The last confirmed pair was killed on Eldey, Iceland, in June 1844.

interestingFacts: The Great Auk was the only flightless member of the auk family.
The name 'penguin' was once used for the Great Auk before it became associated with Southern Hemisphere penguins.

period.label: Historical era

extinction.label: Last captive quagga died in 1883
extinction.note: The quagga is generally treated as an extinct subspecies of the plains zebra.

causes.claim: Hunting for hides and meat, along with conversion of its range to livestock pasture, caused its disappearance.

habitat.text: Dry grasslands and scrub in the Cape region.

geographicRange.text: South Africa, especially the former Cape Province.

animals.livingRelatives: The plains zebra (Equus quagga) survives. The quagga is generally classified as an extinct subspecies of that species, not a separate living lineage.
animals.fossilDiscoveries: Historical skins, mounted specimens, and written records document the quagga's coat and its former range in South Africa.
animals.appearance: A plains zebra subspecies with bold stripes on the head, neck, and forebody that became faint toward the hindquarters.
animals.diet: Grazing herbivore.

size.text: A medium-sized plains zebra.
size.estimate: Exact body dimensions varied and are not summarized here.

lastKnownRecord.text: The last known captive quagga died at Amsterdam Zoo on 12 August 1883; wild disappearance came earlier.

interestingFacts: The quagga is not a separate living zebra species; it is usually classified as an extinct subspecies of Equus quagga.
Historical images and surviving mounted specimens document its distinctive coat pattern.

period.label: Late Cretaceous - about 68-66 million years ago

extinction.label: Disappeared at the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary, about 66 million years ago
extinction.note: No individual last animal is known.

causes.claim: The end-Cretaceous mass extinction eliminated all non-avian dinosaurs.
The Chicxulub impact was the primary trigger of the global extinction event.

habitat.text: Late Cretaceous floodplains and coastal lowlands of western North America.

geographicRange.text: Western North America, including present-day Canada and the United States.

animals.livingRelatives: Birds are living theropod dinosaurs, but no bird is a direct descendant of Tyrannosaurus rex; they share a much older dinosaur ancestry.
animals.fossilDiscoveries: Fossils from western North America include bones, teeth, and partial to substantial skeletons. The species was named in 1905 after earlier discoveries, including remains found in 1902.
animals.appearance: A large bipedal theropod with a massive skull, powerful jaws, and short forelimbs.
animals.diet: Carnivore; fossil evidence includes bite marks on other dinosaurs.

size.text: About 12 m long for a typical adult.
size.estimate: Length and mass are estimates and vary between individuals.

lastKnownRecord.text: No individual last record is known; its fossils occur in rocks near the end-Cretaceous boundary.

interestingFacts: The name Tyrannosaurus rex means 'tyrant lizard king.'
Some bones first named Manospondylus gigas were later recognized as belonging to Tyrannosaurus rex.

size.estimate: Length is a reconstruction-based estimate.

period.label: Late Cretaceous - about 99-93.5 million years ago

extinction.label: Fossil record ends in the Late Cretaceous; exact disappearance date is unknown
extinction.note: The fossil record is incomplete and does not identify a last individual.

causes.claim: A specific cause for the disappearance of Spinosaurus aegyptiacus has not been established.

habitat.text: North African coastal wetlands, tidal flats, and river systems are represented in its fossil setting.
habitat.confidence: supported; detailed lifestyle interpretations remain debated

geographicRange.text: Fossils attributed to Spinosaurus are known from Egypt and Morocco.

animals.livingRelatives: Birds are the living dinosaurs, but no living animal is a direct descendant of Spinosaurus.
animals.fossilDiscoveries: The original Egyptian fossils were destroyed during the Second World War. Later North African finds, including material from Morocco, have informed reconstructions, while some identifications remain debated.
animals.appearance: A large theropod with an elongated, narrow snout, short hind limbs, a tall back sail, and a deep tail.
animals.diet: Carnivore; fish are strongly indicated by its jaw and tooth form, but the full diet is uncertain.

size.text: About 14 m long in the Natural History Museum directory.
size.estimate: The estimate is uncertain because no complete skeleton is known.

lastKnownRecord.text: No individual last record is known; the fossil record is incomplete.

interestingFacts: The first known Spinosaurus fossils were destroyed during the Second World War.
Scientists continue to debate how much time Spinosaurus spent swimming versus living near water.

image.creator: Connor Ashbridge

period.label: Miocene to Pliocene

extinction.label: Fossil record ends about 3.6 million years ago
extinction.note: The last fossil occurrence is not a precise date of the last living animal.

causes.claim: Cooling oceans and changes in prey distribution may have reduced suitable habitat.
Competition with other predators may have contributed.

habitat.text: Warm coastal and open-ocean waters.

geographicRange.text: Fossil teeth have been found in marine deposits on several continents.

animals.livingRelatives: Megalodon has no living descendants. Modern sharks are relatives within cartilaginous fishes, but the great white shark is not a surviving Megalodon.
animals.fossilDiscoveries: Abundant fossil teeth and some vertebrae occur in marine deposits worldwide. No complete Megalodon skeleton is known because shark skeletons are mostly cartilage.
animals.appearance: A giant extinct mackerel shark known especially from its abundant, robust fossil teeth.
animals.diet: Carnivore; fossil evidence includes bite marks on marine mammals.

size.text: A very large shark; published maximum lengths vary widely.
size.estimate: Body length is reconstructed from teeth and vertebrae; no complete skeleton is known.

lastKnownRecord.text: The youngest widely accepted fossil occurrences are approximately 3.6 million years old.

interestingFacts: Megalodon is known largely from teeth because shark skeletons are mostly cartilage.
Its exact size remains a subject of scientific study.

extinction.label: Exact species-level disappearance date is not established
extinction.note: The name refers to an early marine reptile; the genus is not a dinosaur.

causes.claim: A specific cause for the disappearance of Plesiosaurus dolichodeirus is not known.

habitat.text: Marine waters.

geographicRange.text: Fossils are especially associated with Early Jurassic deposits in southern England.

animals.livingRelatives: No plesiosaur survives. Living reptiles are distant relatives within the broader reptile lineage, not descendants of Plesiosaurus.
animals.fossilDiscoveries: Early Jurassic fossils from Lyme Regis and nearby Dorset, England, include important Plesiosaurus material collected during the 19th century.
animals.appearance: A marine reptile with a broad body, four paddle-like limbs, and a long neck.
animals.diet: Likely fed on fish and other marine animals; diet is inferred from anatomy and associated fossils.

size.text: A few metres long in commonly described specimens.
size.estimate: Individual size estimates vary with the fossil and reconstruction.

lastKnownRecord.text: No last individual is documented; the species is known from Early Jurassic fossils.

interestingFacts: Plesiosaurus was a marine reptile, not a dinosaur.
Its long neck and four paddles distinguish it from the long-snouted pliosaurs.

period.label: Silurian

extinction.label: Species-level last appearance is not established
extinction.note: Trilobites as a whole survived much later and disappeared at the end-Permian extinction; that group-level date is not this species' extinction date.

causes.claim: The exact cause and date of disappearance of Calymene blumenbachii are not established.

habitat.text: Marine seafloor.

geographicRange.text: Silurian fossils are known from Wales and other parts of the United Kingdom.

animals.livingRelatives: Trilobites have no living members. Modern arthropods such as insects, crustaceans, and arachnids are relatives at the broad phylum level, not surviving trilobites.
animals.fossilDiscoveries: Calymene blumenbachii is represented in Silurian limestone fossils from Wales, including material from the Dudley area; specimens are often called 'Dudley locusts.'
animals.appearance: An arthropod with a segmented, three-lobed mineralized exoskeleton.
animals.diet: Not firmly established for this species.

size.text: Fossil specimens vary in size.
size.estimate: No single species-wide size estimate is provided.

lastKnownRecord.text: Silurian fossils document the species; a final individual is not known.

interestingFacts: The name 'trilobite' refers to the three longitudinal lobes of the body.
Some Calymene fossils are informally called 'Dudley locusts.'

extinction.label: Disappeared by 1768, about 27 years after its scientific description
extinction.confidence: historically documented; exact last individual unknown
extinction.note: The species was described during Vitus Bering's 1741 expedition.

causes.claim: Intensive hunting by people for meat and other products caused its rapid extinction.

habitat.text: Cold coastal waters and kelp beds of the Commander Islands.

geographicRange.text: Known historically from the Commander Islands in the Bering Sea; fossil evidence indicates a wider former range.

animals.livingRelatives: The dugong (Dugong dugon) is the closest living relative; manatees are also living sirenians.

animals.appearance: A massive, slow-moving sirenian with thick skin, a broad tail, and no functional teeth.
animals.diet: Herbivore; fed on kelp and other marine vegetation.

size.text: Very large, with historical estimates reaching several tonnes in mass.
size.estimate: Length and mass values are uncertain because complete measurements are rare.

lastKnownRecord.text: Historical accounts indicate the species was gone by 1768; an exact last individual is not documented.

interestingFacts: Steller's sea cow was the largest member of the order Sirenia known in the historical record.
Its extinction was exceptionally rapid after contact with maritime hunters.

animals.fossilDiscoveries: A partial skeleton from Luzon was recovered in deposits dated to about 709,000 years ago. Fossil bones from Rizal, Kalinga show cut and percussion marks. The species was historically called Rhinoceros philippinensis and is now placed in Nesorhinus.
animals.appearance: A small-bodied extinct rhinoceros known from fossil bones and teeth; life appearance is reconstructed from its skeletal remains.
animals.diet: Herbivore; rhinoceroses feed on plant material, though the exact diet of this species is not fully known.

size.text: Research indicates a comparatively small-bodied island rhinoceros.
size.estimate: Species-specific body mass estimates vary; no single figure is used here.

lastKnownRecord.text: Fossil evidence from Luzon includes remains dated to approximately 709,000 years ago; this is not necessarily the final appearance of the species.

interestingFacts: The species is an important part of the Philippine Pleistocene fossil record.
A fossil skeleton from Kalinga was found with evidence of butchery by early humans.

causes.claim: The cause of extinction is not established by the available evidence.

habitat.text: Terrestrial island environments on Luzon; detailed habitat preferences are uncertain.

geographicRange.text: Luzon, Philippines, including fossil localities in Kalinga, Cagayan, and Antipolo.

animals.livingRelatives: Living tortoises are relatives within Testudines, but no living species is a descendant of Megalochelys sondaari.
animals.fossilDiscoveries: Fossils include pieces of the carapace and other skeletal remains. The National Museum of the Philippines documents specimens from Liwan in Kalinga, Tuao in Cagayan, and Antipolo.
animals.appearance: A giant land tortoise known from fossil shell and skeletal remains; the exact full-body appearance is reconstructed from those remains.
animals.diet: Likely herbivorous, as in other giant land tortoises; species-specific dietary evidence is limited.

size.text: A giant tortoise relative; a reliable species-specific shell length is not supplied here.
size.estimate: Do not substitute measurements from other Megalochelys species.

lastKnownRecord.text: Known from Early Pleistocene fossil deposits; no exact final occurrence is established.

interestingFacts: Its fossils have been found at several localities on Luzon.
The species is included in the National Museum of the Philippines' extinct megafauna collection.
